event_description: Winter Storm (December 26-27 (Winter Storm))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm system brought wide spread precipitation to Northwest Kansas, beginning on the 26th.  The precipitation began as rain then transitioned to snow during the night of the 26th.  Winds became strong as the rain changed over to snow the night of the 26th.  This caused blizzard conditions to occur in the snowfall.  The blizzard conditions swept northeast across Northwest Kansas, ending as the snowfall shifted east.  Multiple accidents and slide-offs were reported on I-70 in Gove County due to the icy roadway and poor visibility.  One of the accidents involved a fatality.  The highest snowfall amount reported was 9.5 southwest of Hoxie.||Besides the snow, high wind gusts also occurred.  A gust of 58 MPH was measured at the Goodland airport, and a 60 MPH gust was measured at the Hill City airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Similar wind speeds and radar imagery were observed across Decatur County compared to  neighboring counties with reports of blizzard conditions.

event_description: Winter Storm (December 26-27 (Winter Storm))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A closed upper level low lifted northeast across the 4-corners region and deepened as it crossed into western Kansas. An attendant cold front pushed into west-central and extreme southwest Kansas as deep low-level moisture continued to advect into the region. Rain showers began on the evening of the 26th, and transitioned to snow behind the front with strong northwest winds. Blizzard conditions were reported throughout the region, leaving roads closed and motorists stranded.  Snowfall in excess of 10 inches was widespread from near Elkhart, through Lakin and Garden City and up to near Scott City and Dighton.  There were several reports of 12 inches.  Snow drifts were over six feet at many locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Near zero visibility in heavy snow and blowing snow.  Visibility was limited to 400 feet.

event_description: Winter Storm (December 26-27 (Winter Storm))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The first true near-blizzard to blizzard conditions of the 2018-19 winter season struck mainly Phillips and Rooks counties in western portions of North Central Kansas on this Thursday, causing not only many of the usual winter storm disruptions, but also snarling post-Christmas travel. Snow totals themselves were not very impressive, with reports from a combination of NWS cooperative observers and CoCoRaHS observers including: 2.5 at Logan, 2.2 east of Phillipsburg and 1.3 near Plainville. However, snowfall analysis maps and satellite imagery strongly suggest that far northwestern Phillips County likely received at least 3-4. Farther east, most of the remainder of this six-county area saw well under 1, if hardly any at all. That being said, winds were certainly a major factor, as much of the 27th featured sustained north-northwest speeds of 25-35 MPH and frequent gusts of 40-50 MPH, resulting in considerable blowing snow and reducing visibilities to well-under one mile at times. ||Breaking down event timing, and initially backing up a bit, this storm started off very similar to the one four weeks prior, and with something fairly unusual for this time of year: soaking winter rain! In fact, Wednesday the 26th featured widespread rainfall of 1-2 across all of North Central Kansas. As colder air invaded late that night, rain quickly changed to snow, with at least near-blizzard conditions already reported by sunrise in Phillips/Rooks counties. However, the majority of accumulating snow and overall-worst conditions focused between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m., with very little snow thereafter. In the mid-upper levels, the primary player was a powerful, large scale trough, with its center tracking from NM on the 26th, to western KS by daybreak on the 27th, then northward across eastern NE into MN during the afternoon and evening. The associated strong surface low pressure system started the morning of the 27th over central Kansas (pressure around 996 millibars), before steadily marching to around Kansas City by mid-day and the IA/MN border by evening. On a climate-related side note, this event put an exclamation point on an incredibly wet December, as most of North Central Kansas received between 2.50-3.50 of precipitation for the month, or generally 300-500% of normal! For most official stations, it was a Top-3 wettest December on record, and was the outright-wettest at places such as Beloit.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snowfall of 2.5 inches occurred in Logan (NWS coop observer) and 2.2 inches occurred six miles east of Phillipsburg (CoCoRaHS). Wind gusts frequently reached 40 to 50 mph during the snow, frequently bringing visibility down to a quarter mile or less.

event_description: State of disaster emergency for severe storms and flooding after widespread torrential rainfall
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of supercell thunderstorms developed along a slow moving cold front, during the afternoon and evening of May 6th, 2019 into the early morning hours of May 7th. The supercells produced large hail and some damaging winds. As the storms moved south, they began to stall over southern Kansas and produce some flash flooding.  Significant flooding started during the late night hours of May 7th, 2019 when Chanute picked up 5 to 6 inches of rainfall in only a couple hours. This caused widespread flash flooding across the city where numerous water rescues took place.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous tree branches were reported down.

event_description: State of disaster emergency for severe storms and flooding after widespread torrential rainfall
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A elevated thunderstorms produced severe hail in a few spots from late morning into early afternoon on this Monday. These storms occurred with surface temperatures not usually associated with thunderstorms. Around sunrise, a northwest-southeast oriented line of showers moved into north central Kansas. Movement was northeast. Around 930 AM CST, a thunderstorm developed over eastern Phillips county, just behind this line. This storm quickly became severe, dropping 1 inch hail across northern Smith county until 1130 AM CST. The storm then crossed the border into Nebraska. A couple more thunderstorms developed over north central Kansas through midday and into the early afternoon. These storms were not severe until storm mergers along the state line resulted in the formation of a short line of storms that crossed Jewell county between 115 PM and 230 PM CST. This line produced 1 inch hail near Formoso.||A cool air mass was over the region. Temperatures were near 60. A strong, but slow-moving, cold front had moved through the previous night and become stationary near Interstate 70. In the upper-levels, the flow was zonal over the central and eastern U.S., with a broad trough extending into the north central United States from Canada. The mid-level lapse rate was around 8 C/km, with MUCAPE between 500-1000 J/kg. The freezing level was relatively low (around 10,000 ft AGL). Effective deep layer shear was 30-35 kt. These storms appeared to be associated with frontogenesis along the 850 mb front, and warm air advection from 850-700 mb.

event_description: State of disaster emergency for severe storms and flooding after widespread torrential rainfall
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled frontal boundary was draped across portions of Kansas during the day on May 7th, 2019 ahead of an approaching storm system. Widespread showers and thunderstorms with very heavy rainfall developed across the area. These storms inundated areas that were already saturated from recent rainfall resulting in widespread flooding across south central Kansas. ||Significant flash flooding occurred during the evening and overnight of May 7th, 2019 into the early morning hours of May 8th. The most significant flash flooding occurred during the early morning hours of May 8th, when areas southeast of Wichita picked up between seven and ten inches of rainfall in a 24 hour period. Numerous water rescues took place across Mulvane, Augusta, Wellington and Rose Hill. In addition, several miles of the Kansas Turnpike was closed south of Mulvane due to the Slate Creek reaching record levels. Closing this much of the Kansas Turnpike due to flooding hasn't happened in over 30 years.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: County dispatch reported numerous road closures due to high water.

event_description: State of disaster emergency for severe storms and flooding after widespread torrential rainfall
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A elevated thunderstorms produced severe hail in a few spots from late morning into early afternoon on this Monday. These storms occurred with surface temperatures not usually associated with thunderstorms. Around sunrise, a northwest-southeast oriented line of showers moved into north central Kansas. Movement was northeast. Around 930 AM CST, a thunderstorm developed over eastern Phillips county, just behind this line. This storm quickly became severe, dropping 1 inch hail across northern Smith county until 1130 AM CST. The storm then crossed the border into Nebraska. A couple more thunderstorms developed over north central Kansas through midday and into the early afternoon. These storms were not severe until storm mergers along the state line resulted in the formation of a short line of storms that crossed Jewell county between 115 PM and 230 PM CST. This line produced 1 inch hail near Formoso.||A cool air mass was over the region. Temperatures were near 60. A strong, but slow-moving, cold front had moved through the previous night and become stationary near Interstate 70. In the upper-levels, the flow was zonal over the central and eastern U.S., with a broad trough extending into the north central United States from Canada. The mid-level lapse rate was around 8 C/km, with MUCAPE between 500-1000 J/kg. The freezing level was relatively low (around 10,000 ft AGL). Effective deep layer shear was 30-35 kt. These storms appeared to be associated with frontogenesis along the 850 mb front, and warm air advection from 850-700 mb.

event_description: Wildfire (October 20 - November 5 (Wildfire))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: This Sunday was one of the windiest days of fall 2022 within this six-county North Central Kansas area, with most of the afternoon-evening featuring south-southwesterly sustained speeds commonly 30-40 MPH and frequent gusts 45-55 MPH (localized 58+ MPH). Fortunately, the local area managed to avoid any notable wildfire activity (albeit not by much, as two sizable fires ignited within five miles of the state line in far south central Nebraska). However, this area did endure a healthy dose of blowing dust, with at least a few hours of widespread visibility reductions to one mile or less, and more localized reductions to less than one-quarter mile (even near-zero). In tandem with the strong winds, the stage was set for the blowing dust thanks to unseasonably-warm temperatures and very dry conditions, with the majority of North Central Kansas in the midst of longer-term drought ranging from Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2),and with worse drought conditions including Exceptional (D4) noted in the dust's primary southwestern Kansas source region. Although impacts from the strong winds/blowing dust indeed materialized, fortunately the local area was spared the possibility of a more widespread severe thunderstorm threat. Despite roughly the eastern half of the area being assigned a Marginal to Slight Risk of severe storms by SPC, convective development proved to be very spotty/weak overall, with only one (unverified) Severe Thunderstorm Warning issued for parts of Mitchell/Jewell counties. The day's biggest story locally was the blowing dust, which mainly concentrated between 2-6 p.m. CDT and during which time a Blowing Dust Advisory was in effect for all six counties. In addition, a more urgent Dust Storm Warning was issued for parts of Rooks, Osborne, Smith and Phillips counties mainly 2:30-4:00 p.m. CDT. Though ground-truth reports were limited, law enforcement reported near-zero visibility in the Stockton area, mainly resulting from larger-scale dust plumes surging up into the local area from the southwest. Getting back to the strong south/southwest winds themselves...most of the unofficial sensors within North Central Kansas clocked peak gusts of 45-55 MPH. However, there were isolated higher gusts that approached/barely breached High Wind criteria, including: 59 MPH near Beloit and 57 MPH in Plainville and Tipton. There were no known reports of significant wind damage.  ||Concluding with a closer look at the meteorological setup on the 23rd, the main player in the mid-upper levels was an expansive/deep trough slowly shifting from the Intermountain West into the Central Rockies over the course of the day. At the surface, the day began with a 988 millibar low pressure center over northeast CO. By early afternoon, an elongated, southwest-northeast oriented trough axis intensified to 986 millibars from northeast CO to far north central NE, with North Central Kansas firmly in the warm sector and within a tightening surface pressure gradient. This gradient, in tandem with steep low-mid level lapse rates and resultant deep mixing, drove the persistent 45-55 MPH gusts throughout the afternoon and early evening, with a subtle pre-frontal trough causing local winds to average more true southerly east of the Highway 281 corridor and more southwesterly to the west. The deep mixing also allowed temperatures to soar and dewpoints/relative humidity to plummet. High temperatures across most of North Central Kansas topped out in the upper 80s-low 90s (around 25 degrees above normal), while relative humidity values plunged to between 15-25 percent across most of the area during the mid-late afternoon. Strong south-southwest winds persisted after sunset, but by late evening the primary surface low migrated into the eastern Dakotas, allowing a trailing cold front to enter far western portions of the local area...turning winds northwesterly and easing gusts to more manageable levels as it passed. By around 2 a.m. CDT on the 24th, this front finally cleared the far southeastern fringes of North Central Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust of 59 MPH was measured by an unofficial mesonet station located five miles south-southeast of Beloit.

event_description: Wildfire (October 20 - November 5 (Wildfire))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout October 2022, portions of four of the six North Central Kansas counties were assigned Severe Drought (D2) by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). This marked the ninth consecutive month that D2 plagued parts of the local area. Following encouraging September precipitation trends for much of the area (roughly three-fourths of locations had above normal Sept. rainfall), October was overall dry area-wide...see below for more Oct. precipitation details. Focusing on county-level USDM drought category specifics, October opened with the majority of the six counties under a varied mix of Moderate Drought (D1) and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions, with most of the D0 focused within Jewell, Mitchell and northern Smith counties. On the best-off side of things, much of central/southern Mitchell County was actually void of all drought categories whatsoever. However, of greatest concern were various swaths of D2 within the four western local counties, impacting: 1) much of the northern halves of Rooks/Osborne counties along with most of far southern Phillips/Smith counties...2) a narrow stripe across extreme southern Rooks/Osborne counties...3) a narrow swath through far western Phillips County. Over the course of the month, drought categories were actually stable/unchanged in most places (including all D2 areas). However, late in the month some one-category degradation occurred mainly within the eastern half of the area, as existing D0 within all of Smith/Osborne and most of Jewell counties degraded to D1, while those portions of Mitchell County void of all drought categories assumed D0. As a result, at month's end D0 was present across most of Mitchell and southeastern Jewell counties. ||Turning to October 2022 precipitation details, unfortunately not only did ALL of North Central Kansas receive below normal amounts, but around 90 percent of the area measured less than one-half of normal (generally less than 1 inch) and around one-third of the area tallied LESS THAN ONE-FOURTH OF NORMAL (generally less than 0.50). Overall, most locations measured somewhere between 0.35-1.00. On the worst off side of things were western portions of Phillips/Rooks counties, where paltry totals per NWS/CoCoRaHS observers included merely 0.15 in Logan (7th-driest October on record out of 72 years) and 0.20 near Webster State Park. On the wettest (but still below normal) side of things, some of the highest measured amounts focused within Jewell and southern Rooks counties, led by 1.03 near Plainville and 0.98 in Formoso. Concluding with a look at increasingly-concerning longer-term drought trends, the majority of North Central Kansas racked up cumulative precipitation deficits of 10-18 inches during the 19-month period between April 2021-Oct. 2022 (precipitation amounts generally 60-80% of normal). Versus normal, and despite official drought categories, one of the most dire totals of all during that 19-month stretch was actually in Beloit, where the NWS Coop Observer tallied 35.06 (17.90 below normal/66% of normal).

event_description: Wildfire (October 20 - November 5 (Wildfire))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout October 2022, portions of four of the six North Central Kansas counties were assigned Severe Drought (D2) by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). This marked the ninth consecutive month that D2 plagued parts of the local area. Following encouraging September precipitation trends for much of the area (roughly three-fourths of locations had above normal Sept. rainfall), October was overall dry area-wide...see below for more Oct. precipitation details. Focusing on county-level USDM drought category specifics, October opened with the majority of the six counties under a varied mix of Moderate Drought (D1) and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions, with most of the D0 focused within Jewell, Mitchell and northern Smith counties. On the best-off side of things, much of central/southern Mitchell County was actually void of all drought categories whatsoever. However, of greatest concern were various swaths of D2 within the four western local counties, impacting: 1) much of the northern halves of Rooks/Osborne counties along with most of far southern Phillips/Smith counties...2) a narrow stripe across extreme southern Rooks/Osborne counties...3) a narrow swath through far western Phillips County. Over the course of the month, drought categories were actually stable/unchanged in most places (including all D2 areas). However, late in the month some one-category degradation occurred mainly within the eastern half of the area, as existing D0 within all of Smith/Osborne and most of Jewell counties degraded to D1, while those portions of Mitchell County void of all drought categories assumed D0. As a result, at month's end D0 was present across most of Mitchell and southeastern Jewell counties. ||Turning to October 2022 precipitation details, unfortunately not only did ALL of North Central Kansas receive below normal amounts, but around 90 percent of the area measured less than one-half of normal (generally less than 1 inch) and around one-third of the area tallied LESS THAN ONE-FOURTH OF NORMAL (generally less than 0.50). Overall, most locations measured somewhere between 0.35-1.00. On the worst off side of things were western portions of Phillips/Rooks counties, where paltry totals per NWS/CoCoRaHS observers included merely 0.15 in Logan (7th-driest October on record out of 72 years) and 0.20 near Webster State Park. On the wettest (but still below normal) side of things, some of the highest measured amounts focused within Jewell and southern Rooks counties, led by 1.03 near Plainville and 0.98 in Formoso. Concluding with a look at increasingly-concerning longer-term drought trends, the majority of North Central Kansas racked up cumulative precipitation deficits of 10-18 inches during the 19-month period between April 2021-Oct. 2022 (precipitation amounts generally 60-80% of normal). Versus normal, and despite official drought categories, one of the most dire totals of all during that 19-month stretch was actually in Beloit, where the NWS Coop Observer tallied 35.06 (17.90 below normal/66% of normal).

event_description: Wildland Fire (March 31 - April 11 (Wildland Fire))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout March 2023, at least portions of four of the six North Central Kansas counties continued to be assigned Severe Drought (D2) by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). This marked the 14th consecutive month that D2 plagued parts of the local area. Unfortunately, following some encouraging recent precipitation trends during January-February, March ushered in renewed disappointment as the entire area registered WELL below normal precipitation (see below for more March precipitation details). Focusing on county-level USDM drought category specifics during March, there was overall-little change within North Central Kansas as a whole, including no change whatsoever to the D2 area. As a result, the month opened and closed with D2 afflicting all of Rooks County, along with roughly the western two-thirds of Osborne County, the southwestern half of Phillips County and a narrow strip of southern Smith County. Elsewhere within the six-county domain, Moderate Drought (D1) persisted within the majority of other locations throughout March, including most of Smith and Jewell counties, roughly the northeast half of Phillips County, the eastern third of Osborne County and a small portion of northwestern Mitchell County. On the first USDM release of the month (valid March 7th), D1 was expanded southeastward to include more of Mitchell County along with the remainder of Jewell County. Following this early-month degradation, the only remaining zone of overall-best-off Abnormally Dry (D0) within the area was confined to parts of eastern Mitchell County.||Turning to March 2023 precipitation details, the entirety of North Central Kansas tallied significantly below normal precipitation, just with some places worse off than others. The majority of the six-county area totaled between 0.20 and 0.40 inch, or roughly 15-30 percent of normal. In fact, not only did almost the entire area receive less than one-third of normal March precipitation, but around 75% of it received no more than one-fourth of normal. Although there were really no winners to speak of, if anything the overall-highest monthly amounts tended to favor Jewell, Mitchell and Smith counties. Per around 20 NWS and CoCoRaHS observers, some of the highest March tallies featured only: 0.49 at Lovewell Dam, 0.44 ten miles south-southwest of Beloit and 0.41 near Hunter. On the very driest side of things, a few of the lowest March totals included: 0.09 in Natoma, 0.21 six miles east of Phillipsburg and 0.22 seven miles north-northeast of Natoma.

event_description: Wildland Fire (March 31 - April 11 (Wildland Fire))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During April 2023, at least portions of five of the six North Central Kansas counties continued to be (or were newly) assigned at least Severe Drought (D2) by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). This marked the 15th consecutive month that D2 plagued parts of the local area. However, of greater concern during the month was the introduction of both Extreme Drought (D3) and worst-off Exceptional Drought (D4) into mainly southwestern parts of the area. This marked the first appearance of D3 anywhere within North Central Kansas in nearly 9 years (since June 2014) and the first instance of D4 in the area in over 9.5 years (since August 2013). It is little surprise that the drought situation went further downhill during the month, given that a very dry March was immediately followed by an exceptionally dry April (see below for more April precipitation details). Focusing on county-level USDM drought category specifics during the month, things opened with D2 covering all of Rooks County, along with roughly the western two-thirds of Osborne County, the southwestern half of Phillips County and a narrow strip of southern Smith County. Elsewhere within the six-county domain, Moderate Drought (D1) was present to start April in nearly all other places, except for a lingering zone of overall-best-off Abnormally Dry D0 within eastern Mitchell County. However, degradation got underway already on the April 11th USDM issuance, as D3 was introduced to southern portions of Rooks/Osborne counties, D2 expanded eastward into western Mitchell County, and eastern Mitchell County went from D0 to D1. Through the rest of the month, the entire D1 area and most of the D2 area remained unchanged, but the D3 zone expanded northward and D4 was introduced to far southwest locales. More specifically, by the April 25th USDM, D4 was present across much of the southern two-thirds of Rooks County along with southwestern Osborne County, and a narrow buffer zone of D3 extended northward into more of Rooks, Osborne, southwestern Phillips and extreme southwestern Mitchell counties. At month's end, only Jewell County remained void of D2-or-worse. ||Turning to April 2023 precipitation details, it was overall bad news, with all of North Central Kansas registering between moderately and tremendously-below normal precipitation. More specifically, the majority of the six-county domain totaled between 0.15-0.90 inch, or roughly 5-40 percent of normal. In fact, around 95 percent of the area measured less than one-half of monthly normals, and roughly 85% of it registered less than ONE-FOURTH of normal! Some official, long-term NWS stations bemoaned a Top-5 driest April on record, including Plainville 4WNW (0.06...THE DRIEST on record out of 114) and Beloit (0.43...2nd-driest out of 115). Per around 20 NWS and CoCoRaHS observers, some of the most dire April tallies included: 0.06 four miles west north-west of Plainville, 0.08 ten miles west-northwest of Stockton, 0.10 at Webster Dam and 0.14 in Cawker City. On the slightly more fortunate (but still well below normal side of things), a few of the highest monthly totals featured: 1.24 ten miles south-southwest of Beloit, 0.92 at Lovewell Dam and 0.87 in Natoma.

event_description: Wildland Fires (April 12-26 (Wildland Fires))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During April 2023, at least portions of five of the six North Central Kansas counties continued to be (or were newly) assigned at least Severe Drought (D2) by the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). This marked the 15th consecutive month that D2 plagued parts of the local area. However, of greater concern during the month was the introduction of both Extreme Drought (D3) and worst-off Exceptional Drought (D4) into mainly southwestern parts of the area. This marked the first appearance of D3 anywhere within North Central Kansas in nearly 9 years (since June 2014) and the first instance of D4 in the area in over 9.5 years (since August 2013). It is little surprise that the drought situation went further downhill during the month, given that a very dry March was immediately followed by an exceptionally dry April (see below for more April precipitation details). Focusing on county-level USDM drought category specifics during the month, things opened with D2 covering all of Rooks County, along with roughly the western two-thirds of Osborne County, the southwestern half of Phillips County and a narrow strip of southern Smith County. Elsewhere within the six-county domain, Moderate Drought (D1) was present to start April in nearly all other places, except for a lingering zone of overall-best-off Abnormally Dry D0 within eastern Mitchell County. However, degradation got underway already on the April 11th USDM issuance, as D3 was introduced to southern portions of Rooks/Osborne counties, D2 expanded eastward into western Mitchell County, and eastern Mitchell County went from D0 to D1. Through the rest of the month, the entire D1 area and most of the D2 area remained unchanged, but the D3 zone expanded northward and D4 was introduced to far southwest locales. More specifically, by the April 25th USDM, D4 was present across much of the southern two-thirds of Rooks County along with southwestern Osborne County, and a narrow buffer zone of D3 extended northward into more of Rooks, Osborne, southwestern Phillips and extreme southwestern Mitchell counties. At month's end, only Jewell County remained void of D2-or-worse.||Turning to April 2023 precipitation details, it was overall bad news, with all of North Central Kansas registering between moderately and tremendously-below normal precipitation. More specifically, the majority of the six-county domain totaled between 0.15-0.90 inch, or roughly 5-40 percent of normal. In fact, around 95 percent of the area measured less than one-half of monthly normals, and roughly 85% of it registered less than ONE-FOURTH of normal! Some official, long-term NWS stations bemoaned a Top-5 driest April on record, including Plainville 4WNW (0.06...THE DRIEST on record out of 114) and Beloit (0.43...2nd-driest out of 115). Per around 20 NWS and CoCoRaHS observers, some of the most dire April tallies included: 0.06 four miles west north-west of Plainville, 0.08 ten miles west-northwest of Stockton, 0.10 at Webster Dam and 0.14 in Cawker City. On the slightly more fortunate (but still well below normal side of things), a few of the highest monthly totals featured: 1.24 ten miles south-southwest of Beloit, 0.92 at Lovewell Dam and 0.87 in Natoma.

event_description: Winter Storms (January 7 -21 (Winter Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The evening of 8 January to the late morning of 9 January, a strong low pressure system pushed through central, south central and southeast Kansas.  Rainfall overspread the region which eventually changed over to snow.  Winter storm warnings were issued for much of central Kansas with winter weather advisories for south central and southeast Kansas.  Much of south central Kansas was later upgraded to a warning.  Many areas of central and south central Kansas experienced heavy snow with very limited visibility during the early morning hours of 9 January given strong winds at the same time.  Snowfall amounts of 5 inches to 12 inches of snow were reported in the Winter Storm Warning area.  Southeast Kansas and far south central Kansas experienced snowfall amounts of 0.1 inches to 2.5 inches.  There were numerous accidents that occurred during the time of this event primarily in south central and southeast Kansas as well as along the I-70 corridor.  Almost all roads were closed across the western half of Kansas by Monday evening, including I-70 west of Salina to the Colorado border. Kansas Highway Patrol responded to nearly 100 calls from motorists during the storm. Strong winds and heavy snow also caused numerous power outages across the region. With the exception of far southeast Kansas, most schools across Kansas cancelled classes, many for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At 7AM on 9 January a COOP Observer reported 1.5 inches of snow in Moran.  Snowfall amounts of 1.5 to 0.1 inches of snow were reported across the county.

Rainfall overspread the region which eventually changed over to snow.  Winter storm warnings were issued for much of central Kansas with winter weather advisories for south central and southeast Kansas.  Much of south central Kansas was later upgraded to a warning.  Many areas of central and south central Kansas experienced heavy snow with very limited visibility during the early morning hours of 9 January given strong winds at the same time.  Snowfall amounts of 5 inches to 12 inches of snow were reported in the Winter Storm Warning area.  Southeast Kansas and far south central Kansas experienced snowfall amounts of 0.1 inches to 2.5 inches. Almost all roads were closed across the western half of Kansas by Monday evening, including I-70 west of Salina to the Colorado border. Kansas Highway Patrol responded to nearly 100 calls from motorists during the storm. Strong winds and heavy snow also caused numerous power outages across the region. With the exception of far southeast Kansas, most schools across Kansas cancelled classes, many for a few days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: At 7AM on 9 January, a COOP observer reported 2 inches of snow in Caldwell.  Snowfall amounts of 2.5 to 0.5 inches were reported across the county.

event_description: Wildland Fires (Feb 26 -Mar 8 (Wildland Fires))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: February 2024 marked the third-consecutive month with widespread above normal precipitation within North Central Kansas, allowing a slow-but-steady improvement in drought conditions to march onward. Nonetheless, at least small sections of five of the six local counties spent the entire month assigned Severe Drought (D2) by the U.S. Drought Monitor, while a small part of a sixth county (Phillips) began the month with D2 before it was removed on the Feb. 13th USDM issuance. In fact, February marked the 25th-consecutive month with D2 afflicting portions of the local area. But focusing on the positive, the biggest news of the month was the removal of Extreme Drought (D3) from western Rooks County on the Feb. 13th USDM...marking the first time in ten months that the entire six-county domain was void of D3. In addition to the D3 removal, February featured a modest reduction in the areal coverage of D2, but also a fairly significant decrease in Moderate Drought (D1) and even a slight increase in places deemed to be void of all drought categories whatsoever. These encouraging trends were spurred on by above normal monthly precipitation across nearly 95 percent of the area...mainly in the form of rain and not snow (see below for more detailed monthly precipitation info). Focusing on February county-level drought category specifics, the month opened with the breakdown as follows: 1) D3 prevailed within parts of the western half of Rooks County (but only constituted around 5% of the total six-county domain)...2) A few splotches of D2 nicked at least small portions of all six counties (but only comprised around 10% of the total area)...3) D1 blanketed roughly 63% of North Central Kansas,  including the vast majority of Jewell, Osborne and Mitchell counties...4) the remaining roughly 22% of the area (almost entirely within Phillips/Smith counties) consisted of a varied mix of D0 and locations deemed void of all drought whatsoever (D-nothing). As the month kicked into gear, it turned out that all improvements (including widespread 1-category and limited 2-category) occurred during the first two USDM issuances of February, with status quo holding firm through the latter half of the month. These early-February improvements were highlighted by: 1) a swath of 2-category improvement (from D3 to D1) over west-central Rooks County...2) a significant reduction in the coverage of D1. In the wake of these welcomed changes, the end-of-month drought category situation stood as follows: 1) A few tiny pockets of D2 lingered within parts of all local counties except Phillips (but constituted merely around 5% of the six-county area)...2) D1 blanketed roughly 44% of North Central Kansas, including the majority of Jewel, Mitchell and Rooks counties...3) D0 covered roughly 41% of the area, including the majority of Smith and Osborne counties...4) the remaining approximately 10% of the area (entirely within northern Phillips/Smith counties) was assigned drought-free D-nothing. ||Turning to February 2024 precipitation details, it was overall excellent news for the third-straight month, as roughly 95% of North Central Kansas tallied at least slightly above normal precipitation (meaning more than roughly 0.82), and around 80% of the area checked in between 140-205% of normal. The overall-wettest areas (greatest concentration of totals around 1.50 or more) resided within the four western-most local counties, while slightly lower (but still mainly above normal amounts) focused within Jewell/Mitchell counties in the east. Per around 30 NWS and CoCoRaHS observers, some of the very-highest monthly totals featured: 2.58 near Damar, 2.05 in Natoma, 1.71 near Plainville and 1.62 at Webster Dam. In fact, the NWS observer near Plainville recorded its 12th-wettest February on record out of 116, and the wettest since 2001. Meanwhile, a few of the lowest (but still near-normal) February precipitation totals included: 0.70 near Scottsville, 0.71 ten miles south-southwest of Beloit and 0.75 in Cawker City. On one final note, despite sites such as the NWS Cooperative Observer in Beloit notching above normal precipitation for the fourth-straight month, long-term deficits remained intact, as Beloit totaled only 60.93 over the 35-month stretch from April 2021-February 2024...24.86 below normal/71% of normal.

Over the course of the month, most of North Central Kansas actually maintained status quo (including all of Phillips/Rooks and most of Smith counties). However, due to the prevailing dryness, decent portions of especially Mitchell/Osborne counties saw one-category degradation, with some places going from D1 to D2, and others going from D0 to D1. On one small positive note, a weather system late in the month on the 25th-26th brought beneficial rainfall of at least 1-3 to parts of especially Jewell and far northeastern Mitchell counties, prompting a few small pockets of one-category improvement. event_description: Wildland Fires (April 5-18 (Wildland Fires))

As a result, for the first time in nearly a year, a calendar month featured greater areal coverage of drought degradation than improvement (per weekly issuances of the U.S. Drought Monitor/USDM). Over the course of the month, most of North Central Kansas actually maintained status quo (including all of Phillips/Rooks and most of Smith counties). event_description: Severe Storms (May 6-9 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of severe thunderstorms moved into far eastern Kansas late in the evening, around 8 PM CST. This line of storms brought numerous reports of wind damage to portions of Leavenworth, Wyandotte, and Johnson County Kansas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A swath of straight-line wind damage occurred near a mesovortex that developed within a line of thunderstorms on the evening of May 6, beginning near Piper in Wyandotte County. Several trees were downed along a path from Donahoo Road to Polfer Road, crossing 123rd Street between Polfer Road and Marxen Road. In this area, several larger trees and limbs were downed, with a couple uprooted. The swath of winds progressed toward Wolcott Drive and Tontine Road, where several trees were downed, snapped, or uprooted. A private weather station reported a 60-mph gust in this area at this time, but stronger winds were likely present given the nature of the tree damage. The damaging winds crossed the Missouri River and reached Missouri State Highway 45 north of Waldron, where multiple small trees or limbs were damaged as well. No discernible damage was noted to the northeast of this area. Damage along the path was all directed to the north- northeast, which corroborates with radar data from the Terminal Doppler Radar at TMCI. This straight-line wind event preceded the tornado that eventually developed near Hoover in Platte County a few minutes later.

event_description: Severe Storms (May 6-9 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Potent upper level low brings widespread severe weather to much of the Central Plains, including portions of north central Kansas, during the afternoon and early evening hours of May 6th. The initial thunderstorms developed in the Norton, KS area between noon and 1PM CDT, then gradually shifted east into Phillips and Rooks Counties between 1-3PM. The initial threat with these more discrete cells was hail up to golf ball size. However, as storms transitioned weaker and more linear after 3PM along and east of Hwy 281, the primary severe hazard became strong to marginally severe wind gusts around 50-60 MPH.  The leading edge of the line of thunderstorms that posed the damaging wind threat largely shifted east of the GID CWA by 6PM CDT. The severe threat persisted through the evening hours for much of eastern Kansas.

Several trees were downed along a path from Donahoo Road to Polfer Road, crossing 123rd Street between Polfer Road and Marxen Road. In this area, several larger trees and limbs were downed, with a couple uprooted. The swath of winds progressed toward Wolcott Drive and Tontine Road, where several trees were downed, snapped, or uprooted. A private weather station reported a 60-mph gust in this area at this time, but stronger winds were likely present given the nature of the tree damage. The damaging winds crossed the Missouri River and reached Missouri State Highway 45 north of Waldron, where multiple small trees or limbs were damaged as well. No discernible damage was noted to the northeast of this area. Damage along the path was all directed to the north- northeast, which corroborates with radar data from the Terminal Doppler Radar at TMCI. This straight-line wind event preceded the tornado that eventually developed near Hoover in Platte County a few minutes later.

This storm tracked east along I-70 producing a few brief tornadoes across Russell and northern Ellsworth county.  As it progressed east, the wind and hail threat ramp-up as it moved into Saline County.  The Salina Airport measured a 100 mph wind gust!  There was also numerous reports of golf ball size hail across Salina. ||A rapidly moving line of storms called a derecho then moved out of western Kansas and into Reno and Kingman counties shortly after 7 pm.  This intense line of storms produced widespread 70 to 90 mph winds as it raced off to the northeast at 70 to 80 mph. Hardest hit were the communities of Hutchinson Haven, Burrton, Halstead and Newton where widespread tree damage and power outages were reported.  Damage was also reported across southern Marion and northern Butler counties with  tornado damage was documented near Burns.  The destructive line of storms continued to produce damaging winds as it tracked toward Kansas City late Sunday night.

event_description: Wildland Fires (October 24 - November 1 (Wildland Fires))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) Drought conditions developed across portions southeastern Kansas through the end of October. Sparse rainfall amounts occurred during the month allowing for the development of drought conditions over portions of southeastern Kansas before a line of storms finally brough more than a few hundredths of an inch to the area just before the end of the month. Many locations saw no rainfall from the last week of September until a line of storms moved through the area on October 30th.  Across southeastern Kansas Severe (D3) drought developed by the middle of the month with an expansion of Severe (D2), Moderate (D1) Drought and abnormally Dry (D0) conditions. The primary impacts of the drought occurred in the agricultural communities. Hay growth was impacted along with reports of crop and vegetation impacts due to limited soil and surface moisture, stock ponds showed impacts and low flows on several streams and rivers were reported. Final reports of damages will be placed in the last month the drought occurred in the counties impacted in 2024.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Limited periods of rainfall through the month allowed Severe (D2) Drought to develop across the County. Impacts across the region occurred over larger scale agriculture. Farm and stock ponds saw impacts with ground water levels falling. Crop and vegetation growth was showed signs of stress due to limited moisture. Monetary crop losses for 2024 will be included in future reports when the drought ends and loses are assessed.

event_description: Winter Storms (January 4 - February 9 (Winter Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A winter storm brought a prolonged period of high impact winter weather to north central and northeast Kansas on January 4th and 5th.  Light freezing drizzle and light freezing rain began Saturday January 4th which due to air temperatures and roadways temperatures in the 20s lead to treacherous driving conditions throughout the region.  The freezing rain eventually transitioned to heavy snow on Sunday January 5th.  Strong winds of 30-40 mph along with heavy snow created blizzard conditions across many areas on Sunday.  Many areas received near record one day snowfall values of 10-18 inches and the majority of state highways became impassable and closed due to the snow and blowing snow.   This was one of the highest impact storms across northeast Kansas in the past decade causing all state and interstate highways in northeast Kansas to be considered closed and impassable by Sunday afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A long duration winter storm event hit the region. All of the area endured freezing drizzle and freezing rain Saturday afternoon and Saturday night January 4th and 5th before changing over to sleet and snow.  Ice accumulations across Anderson County were estimated to be around one quarter to one half of an inch with snowfall amounts of 1 to 4 inches.  A spotter reported around one half inch of ice and 3 inches of snow 5 miles southwest of Harris from this storm.

event_description: Severe Storms (May 18 - 19 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of severe storms impacted much of the eastern half of Kansas during the afternoon hours of May 19th into the early morning hours of the 20th. Additional storms developed across portions of south central Kansas and the Flint Hills during the early evening hours of May 19th. These storms produced up to tennis ball sized hail along with 60 mph winds. Later during the evening and nighttime hours of May 19th, a couple of clusters of storms moved out of western Kansas and into central and south central Kansas. This round of severe storms produced up to 91 mph winds and half-dollar sized hail. ||Additionally, non-thunderstorm high winds occurred across much of south central Kansas behind the final round of severe storms, and several reports of damage along with non-thunderstorm wind gusts up to 72 mph were reported.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tornado formed south of farmstead near River Road, made a glancing blow to the farmstead, then continued NNW toward Hwy 36.  Power poles were broken, a well established cotton wood tree was uprooted, and a well anchored antenna was twisted and bent by the tornado. Another farmstead north of CR M was also impacted by the tornado. The tornado removed the roof and doors from a metal building, relocated a couple grain bins, and leveled a wooden shed. However the tornado turned away from house before continuing north through the windbreak.  The tornado ended before reaching the highway.

event_description: Severe Storms (May 18 - 19 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted many areas of Kansas. The initial round developed during the mid-afternoon hours with numerous large hail reports across central and south-central Kansas. The next round developed during the late afternoon and evening hours, producing large hail across central Kansas. ||The final round developed after 9 PM across west-central Kansas and moved east-northeastward into Reno County. event_description: Severe Storms (May 18 - 19 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Intense late afternoon and early thunderstorms produced large hail and localized flash flooding across a part of north central Kansas. Beloit was hit the hardest as hail reached 2��� in diameter. However, flash flooding thanks to nearly 6��� of rain was the problem in parts of Jewell and Smith counties. Smith County Emergency Management verified county roads flooded north of Lebanon along with water impacting U.S. Highway 281 north of Smith Center. The thunderstorms fired between 4 and 6 pm along in Osborne and Mitchell counties and rolled northeast. Despite the movement of the thunderstorms, eastern Smith and western/northern Jewell county experienced a 2-3 hour period of training thunderstorms dumping heavy rain which resulted in the flooding. Most of the runoff from the rain was in the White Rock Creek Basin and eventually flowed into Lovewell Reservoir. The thunderstorms lifted north into Nebraska by mid-evening. ||Meteorologically speaking, an upper level low pressure system was located in northeast Wyoming. A shortwave moved across Kansas and into south central Nebraska during the late afternoon and evening hours. Surface low pressure in northwest Kansas had weakened some, but there was still ample south and southeast flow to transport low level moisture north resulting in surface dewpoints in the middle 60s as far north as north central Kansas.  Though the deeper low-level moisture and surface instability was located in southern Kansas, strong frontogeneses in the 850-700 mb layer ahead of the short wave sparked a round of storms in the afternoon.  Steep mid-level lapses (8C/KM) and strong effective bulk shear of 60 knots was quite favorable for rapid thunderstorm development. Closer to the instability axis near the Kansas/Nebraska border, large hail from elevated thunderstorms was the primary hazard initially, but slightly drier air to the north (sub 60-degree surface dewpoints) supported a localized wind damage risk with a second round of thunderstorms even after dark. Though the risk for tornadoes was greater to the south, strong low-level wind shear and an eventual transition to bowing line segments did become more favorable for brief tornadoes to form for a time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms dropped as much as 4 to 6 inches of heavy rain across the area. Rural roads in the area were affected by running water, as were a portion of Highway 78/128 near the border of Webster County, NE and Jewell County, KS and a portion of Highway 281 in Smith County, KS. Some of the highest measured rain totals included: 5.62 inches from nine miles north-northwest of Burr Oak, KS; 5.61 inches from three miles east of Guide Rock, NE; 5.60 inches from six miles north of Esbon; 4.84 inches from four miles north-northwest of Bostwick.

event_description: Severe Storms (May 18 - 19 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Intense late afternoon and early thunderstorms produced large hail and localized flash flooding across a part of north central Kansas. Beloit was hit the hardest as hail reached 2��� in diameter. However, flash flooding thanks to nearly 6��� of rain was the problem in parts of Jewell and Smith counties. Smith County Emergency Management verified county roads flooded north of Lebanon along with water impacting U.S. Highway 281 north of Smith Center. The thunderstorms fired between 4 and 6 pm along in Osborne and Mitchell counties and rolled northeast. Despite the movement of the thunderstorms, eastern Smith and western/northern Jewell county experienced a 2-3 hour period of training thunderstorms dumping heavy rain which resulted in the flooding. Most of the runoff from the rain was in the White Rock Creek Basin and eventually flowed into Lovewell Reservoir. The thunderstorms lifted north into Nebraska by mid-evening. ||Meteorologically speaking, an upper level low pressure system was located in northeast Wyoming. A shortwave moved across Kansas and into south central Nebraska during the late afternoon and evening hours. Surface low pressure in northwest Kansas had weakened some, but there was still ample south and southeast flow to transport low level moisture north resulting in surface dewpoints in the middle 60s as far north as north central Kansas.  Though the deeper low-level moisture and surface instability was located in southern Kansas, strong frontogeneses in the 850-700 mb layer ahead of the short wave sparked a round of storms in the afternoon.  Steep mid-level lapses (8C/KM) and strong effective bulk shear of 60 knots was quite favorable for rapid thunderstorm development. Closer to the instability axis near the Kansas/Nebraska border, large hail from elevated thunderstorms was the primary hazard initially, but slightly drier air to the north (sub 60-degree surface dewpoints) supported a localized wind damage risk with a second round of thunderstorms even after dark. Though the risk for tornadoes was greater to the south, strong low-level wind shear and an eventual transition to bowing line segments did become more favorable for brief tornadoes to form for a time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail up to two inches in diameter was reported with this round of storms.

Surface low pressure in northwest Kansas had weakened some, but there was still ample south and southeast flow to transport low level moisture north resulting in surface dewpoints in the middle 60s as far north as north central Kansas. event_description: Severe Storms (May 18 - 19 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple rounds of severe weather impacted many areas of Kansas. The initial round developed during the mid-afternoon hours with numerous large hail reports across central and south-central Kansas. The next round developed during the late afternoon and evening hours, producing large hail across central Kansas. ||The final round developed after 9 PM across west-central Kansas and moved east-northeastward into Reno County. A lone supercell thunderstorm tracked across southwest Kansas and eventually moved into Reno County. This storm produced a long track wedge tornado that was on the ground for over 30 miles and had a width around a mile wide. It destroyed three homes near the town of Plevna along with widespread tree and power line damage. This tornado was given an EF-3 rating with the most significant damage just southwest of Plevna. Fortunately there were no injuries or fatalities with this destructive tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Based on the NWS storm survey, the tornado started in Pratt County then went into Stafford County before entering western Reno County. The total track of the tornado was around 32 miles with 21 of those in Reno County. A peak of EF3 damage was found with estimated winds of 155 mph occurring in Stafford and Pratt counties. In Reno County, the peak estimated winds were 145 mph based on a brick exterior home that had all of the exterior walls removed except long entryway. One portion of an interior wall remained. The maximum width was around one mile. This tornado damaged multiple homes to varying degrees in the town of Plevna with damage ranging from EF0 to EF2. Then the torando tracked northeast before going northwest prior to dissipating.

event_description: Severe Storms (May 18 - 19 (Severe Storms))

event_description: Severe Storms (May 18 - 19 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Intense late afternoon and early thunderstorms produced large hail and localized flash flooding across a part of north central Kansas. Beloit was hit the hardest as hail reached 2��� in diameter. However, flash flooding thanks to nearly 6��� of rain was the problem in parts of Jewell and Smith counties. Smith County Emergency Management verified county roads flooded north of Lebanon along with water impacting U.S. Highway 281 north of Smith Center. The thunderstorms fired between 4 and 6 pm along in Osborne and Mitchell counties and rolled northeast. Despite the movement of the thunderstorms, eastern Smith and western/northern Jewell county experienced a 2-3 hour period of training thunderstorms dumping heavy rain which resulted in the flooding. Most of the runoff from the rain was in the White Rock Creek Basin and eventually flowed into Lovewell Reservoir. The thunderstorms lifted north into Nebraska by mid-evening. ||Meteorologically speaking, an upper level low pressure system was located in northeast Wyoming. A shortwave moved across Kansas and into south central Nebraska during the late afternoon and evening hours. Surface low pressure in northwest Kansas had weakened some, but there was still ample south and southeast flow to transport low level moisture north resulting in surface dewpoints in the middle 60s as far north as north central Kansas.  Though the deeper low-level moisture and surface instability was located in southern Kansas, strong frontogeneses in the 850-700 mb layer ahead of the short wave sparked a round of storms in the afternoon.  Steep mid-level lapses (8C/KM) and strong effective bulk shear of 60 knots was quite favorable for rapid thunderstorm development. Closer to the instability axis near the Kansas/Nebraska border, large hail from elevated thunderstorms was the primary hazard initially, but slightly drier air to the north (sub 60-degree surface dewpoints) supported a localized wind damage risk with a second round of thunderstorms even after dark. Though the risk for tornadoes was greater to the south, strong low-level wind shear and an eventual transition to bowing line segments did become more favorable for brief tornadoes to form for a time.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong thunderstorms dropped as much as 4 to 6 inches of heavy rain across the area. Rural roads in the area were affected by running water, as were a portion of Highway 78/128 near the border of Webster County, NE and Jewell County, KS and a portion of Highway 281 in Smith County, KS. Some of the highest measured rain totals included: 5.62 inches from nine miles north-northwest of Burr Oak, KS; 5.61 inches from three miles east of Guide Rock, NE; 5.60 inches from six miles north of Esbon; 4.84 inches from four miles north-northwest of Bostwick.

event_description: Severe Storms (June 18 - 22 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early morning hours of Tuesday June 17th, a line of storms developed into a bow echo as it progressed south. This line of storms produced extremely strong winds as it tracked south, with Hutchinson reporting an 89 mph gust and the Wichita Airport seeing a 102 mph gust! This was the strongest wind gust ever reported at the Wichita Airport.||These extreme winds caused extensive damage with Sedgwick County receiving around 250 reports of power lines being down which resulted in around 85,000 residents with out power. The stronger wind gusts around 50 to 60 mph lasted for around an hour. ||Additional storms developed throughout the day producing wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph,  near four inch hail in Arkansas City and a brief tornado in Harper County. Tree damage was extensive throughout much of Wichita and surrounding areas especially with multiple rounds of strong winds. The hail in Arkansas City was baseball to softball sized which led to damage of vehicles, homes and businesses across town.

This line of storms produced extremely strong winds as it tracked south, with Hutchinson reporting an 89 mph gust and the Wichita Airport seeing a 102 mph gust! This was the strongest wind gust ever reported at the Wichita Airport.||These extreme winds caused extensive damage with Sedgwick County receiving around 250 reports of power lines being down which resulted in around 85,000 residents with out power. The stronger wind gusts around 50 to 60 mph lasted for around an hour. ||Additional storms developed throughout the day producing wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph,  near four inch hail in Arkansas City and a brief tornado in Harper County. Tree damage was extensive throughout much of Wichita and surrounding areas especially with multiple rounds of strong winds. The hail in Arkansas City was baseball to softball sized which led to damage of vehicles, homes and businesses across town.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Estimated 80 mph winds along with nickel sized hail.

event_description: Severe Storms (June 18 - 22 (Severe Storms))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the late afternoon of the 16th, two lines of storms formed, one in northwestern Kansas, the other in eastern Colorado. Additionally, hail up to 1 inch was reported.

event_description: Wildfire (February 15 (Wildfire))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Moderate (D1) drought lingering across far southeastern Kansas but limited precipitation through the month allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to develop across portions of the area. By the end of the month, along with the Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced increasingly dry conditions with drought expanding leaving Severe (D2) drought and Moderate (D1) drought  conditions in the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

event_description: Wildfire (March 12 (Wildfire))

Limited precipitation through the month allowed Severe (D2) Drought conditions to remain across portions of the area. By the end of the month, along with the Severe (D2) Drought conditions, Moderate (D1) Drought and Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained with little changes. The primary impacts of the drought during the winter months is in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Below the monthly average rainfall occurred which produced increasingly dry conditions with drought remaining Severe (D2) drought to Moderate (D1) across the county by the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Losses however, will be determined once the drought improves beyond Severe (D2) Drought conditions and will include mostly any agricultural impacts unless other significant, non-Ag impacts were noted.

event_description: Wildland Fire (April 11 - April 26 (Wildland Fire))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The month began with Severe (D2) drought lingering across portions of far southeastern Kansas. Through the month, the Ozarks saw timely and ample rainfall. As a result, much of the drought area across southeastern Kansas shrank significantly. By the end of the month only small areas Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remained across southern portions of Cherokee County. The primary impacts of the drought during this period came in the form of surface and ground water, including soil moisture in the absence of agricultural activities. Many of the impacts noted included, but were not limited to, dry stock ponds, low stream and river flows, dry top soils which can lead to impacts to spring crop yields, forage production, delayed spring growth and increases in wild fires prior to spring green up. Low flows on some streams and rivers were noted but not widespread. Some limited monetary losses were noted in areas where the drought continued from 2025 but losses will be reported when drought conditions improve past Severe (D2) Drought conditions or the end of the year if any occurred or were reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slightly above the monthly average rainfall fell during the moth. This allowed drought conditions to improve with only Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions remaining in the southern  portions of the county at the end of the month. Impacts across the region were largely limited to farm and stock ponds, stream and river levels and soil moisture with some ground water levels also falling. Little to no losses were incurred despite the drought conditions other than those to ground and surface water levels.

event_description: Severe Weather (May 14 (Severe Weather))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late afternoon, and into the evening, numerous thunderstorms formed over Northwest Kansas in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline. One of them produced hail up to baseball size over and near Goodland. This same storm also produced wind gusts over 80 mph at the Goodland airport. The storm near Goodland produced a brief tornado southwest of Edson as it merged with another storm. As thunderstorms moved eastward, they continued to produce straight-line winds across Thomas, Sheridan, Graham, Norton, and Gove counties.  Over 40 power poles were snapped in Sheridan County, and a machine shed north of Hoxie sustained damage.  Dust storm conditions were reported on the south edge of the thunderstorm activity as the storms moved east over northern Gove County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a personal weather station.

event_description: Severe Weather (June 20 - July 30 (Severe Weather))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms impacted northwest Kansas from the mid-afternoon hours through the late evening hours on the 20th, in vicinity of deepening low pressure over eastern Colorado. Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Measured by a personal weather station.

Thunderstorms started out as more isolated and moved eastward. With time, thunderstorms congealed into a large complex and moved more southeastward. High amounts of atmospheric instability and wind shear supported several higher-end severe weather reports, including baseball size hail in Sheridan County, and up to 100 mph winds in Thomas County.  The inflow winds with the thunderstorm complex were so high they caused dust storm conditions.  Dust storm conditions also occurred with the outflow winds from the thunderstorm complex.  These thunderstorms also produced high rainfall rates for a prolonged amount of time.  This led to flash flooding of a magnitude that had not been seen in decades.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Weatherlink site 12.9 N Selkirk measured 61 mph gust.

event_description: Severe Weather (June 20 - July 30 (Severe Weather))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early evening hours on the 21st, a few clusters of thunderstorms moved southeast across portions of northwest Kansas. Hail up to one inch in diameter occurred in Thomas County, and wind gusts up to 70 mph occurred in Wichita County, downing numerous power poles.  A short lived tornado occurred in far northwest Thomas County on the leading edge of one of the storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several power poles were downed.

event_description: Severe Weather (June 20 - July 30 (Severe Weather))
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated thunderstorm moved east across Wichita County during the early morning hours on the 23rd, producing estimated quarter size hail in Leoti.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The hail size was estimated. The hail damaged some tomato plants.
